newsitem.title: BURMA: Many Burma universities still closed after unrest.
newsitem.headline: Many Burma universities still closed after unrest.

text.p: Burma's top universities and colleges remained closed on Monday, nearly a month after officials shut them down to prevent a recurrence of student unrest, education officials said.

Universities in the capital like Yangon (Rangoon) University, Yangon Institute of Technology (YIT) and the Institute of Medicine as well as Mandalay University in Burma's second city -- all of which were at the heart of last month's demonstrations -- were still closed on Monday when classes were due to resume following December holidays.
But smaller schools outside of Rangoon as well as some trade schools and language institutions have reopened.

"Some universities and colleges where there were no disturbances last month were reopened," a senior official in the Ministry of Education told Reuters. "It's too early to know the attendance, but most students appear to be back on campus."
An official at Taunggyi University in southwestern Shan State told Reuters by telephone that students were back on campus attending classes. He said there was no sign of unrest.
In Rangoon there was no activity seen at Yangon University or YIT. Access to the campus is limited to students and faculty.
Deputy Education Minister Than Nyunt said last week the schools that were involved in the disturbances would stay closed for an indefinite period until the current situation normalised.
He said about 50,000 students across the country would be affected by the closures, and he did not know if the schools would be reopened in time for end-of-term exams scheduled for February.

Most institutes of higher education were shut in early December, several weeks before regular December holidays, after a series of protests when thousands of students took to the street in the biggest anti-government demonstrations seen since 1988.
The ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) seized power in 1988 after quashing the demonstrations in a bloody crackdown that left thousands dead or in jail.
Students were at the heart of the 1988 uprisings. Schools were closed for nearly two years after the 1988 protest, and students feared the recent demonstrations would end in the same result.
One of their demands in last month's demonstrations was for assurance that classes would not be suspended this time.
"We hope the universities are reopened soon," said one YIT student who attended the student rallies but said he was not an active participant. "It's a waste of time for us."
The government has accused the National League for Democracy (NLD) party led by Nobel Peace laureate Aung San Suu Kyi of being involved in and trying to politicise the student demonstrations.
The students were protesting against police brutality, seeking to organise independent unions and demanding greater freedoms.
Suu Kyi has denied the NLD was involved in the student demonstrations, but said on Saturday she supported their efforts.
"We support the aim of the demonstrations since the aim was justice," she told a news conference, saying she also encouraged students to understand politics.

"I never said rise up against the SLORC. What I want them to do is understand politics and be aware of the political situation. Unless students understand about politics there is no guarantee for the future of our country," said Suu Kyi, who has been under virtual house arrest since the protests began on December 3.
